blocks.text: It has so far been clearly established that, of the many places in the Old Testament in which some claim that the fowl kind is treated, none is sufficiently certain. But the matter stands otherwise with the New, where Christ speaks openly of the crowing of the cock and of the hen's affection for her chicks, which she gathers under her wings. To the crowing of the cock belongs Marc. XIII, 35. "Watch therefore, for you do not know when the master of the house will come, in the evening, or at midnight, or at the crowing of the cock, or in the morning." The Evangelist calls the crowing of the cock by a single word, ἀλεκτοροφωνία [alektorophōnia], as others say ἀλεκτρυοφωνία [alektryophōnia], and the Romans gallicinium [cockcrow]. The Glosses of Philoxenus: Ἀλεκτρυοφωνία [Alektryophōnia], gallicinium, galli cantus [cockcrow, the crowing of the cock]. The Hebrews call this very time קריאת הגבר, the cry, or crowing of the cock. Thus in the Talmudic [col. 120] tractate Yoma, ch. 1, fol. 20a: בכל יום תורמים את המזבח בקריאת הגבר או סמוך לו בין לפניו בין לאחריו, "Every day they remove the ashes from the altar at the crowing of the cock, or at the time nearest to it, whether before or after." And fol. 21a: היוצא לדרך קודם קריאת הגבר דמו בראשו, "Whoever sets out on a journey before the crowing of the cock, his blood is upon his own head": that is, he is answerable for his own death if anything goes wrong. And in Shemot Rabbah, chapter 1, concerning the servitude of the Israelites in Egypt: והיו הנוגשים הולכים לבתי השוטרים בהשכמה להוציאן למלאכתן לקריאת הגבר, "And the taskmasters went to the houses of the officers very early in the morning, to bring them out to their work at the crowing of the cock." And a little later: עמד לשעת קריאת הגבר והוציאו מביתו, "He stood by at the hour of the crowing of the cock, to bring him out of his house." The crowing of the cock is properly the time midway between μεσονύκτιον [mesonyktion] and morning, as the Evangelist defines it: "At midnight," he says, "or at cockcrow, or in the morning." Hence Censorinus, in chapter 19, enumerates the parts of the day thus: "There are also several times of night and day marked out and distinguished by their own names, which are found written here and there in the old poets. I shall set them all out in order. I begin from midnight, which is the beginning and the end of the Roman day. The time next to this is called 'after midnight'. Then follows cockcrow, when the cocks begin to crow; then conticinium, when they have fallen silent; then 'before light', and so it is called diluculum [dawn]. Morning, when the light of the sun is seen," etc. Nor otherwise Macrobius, Saturnalia book 1, ch. 3: "The first time of the day is called the declining of midnight, then [II, 689] cockcrow, then conticinium, when both the cocks fall silent and men too are still at rest; then diluculum, that is, when the day begins to be discerned; then morning, when the day is bright," etc. And the old Glosses: Conticinium, ὁ μεταξὺ ἀλεκτρυοφωνίας χρόνος [ho metaxy alektryophōnias chronos], "the time which is between the cockcrows." This makes no sense; rather one should read ὁ μετὰ τὰς ἀλεκτρυοφωνίας χρόνος [ho meta tas alektryophōnias chronos], "the time which is after the cockcrows." These are spoken of in the plural because there are several. For the cock begins to crow from midnight. Then, in the space midway between μεσονύκτιον [mesonyktion] and dawn, it crows again. Therefore many call this crowing the second. Aristophanes in the Ἐκκλησιάζουσαι [Ekklēsiazousai], page 735:
Οὐδ᾽ εἰ μὰ Δία τοτ᾽ ἦλθες, ὅτε τὸ δεύτερον Ἀλεκτρυὼν ἐφθέγγετο. — — — [Oud᾽ ei ma Dia tot᾽ ēlthes, hote to deuteron Alektryōn ephthengeto.]

"Not even, by Jove, if you had come when the cock was crowing for the second time." Heliodorus, book 5: Ἀλεκτρυόνες ἤδη τὸ δεύτερον ᾖδον [Alektryones ēdē to deuteron ēdon], "The cocks were already crowing for the second time." Hence the old proverb among the Paroemiographers, on which Erasmus says much: Πρὶν ἢ τὸ δεύτερον ἀλεκτρυὼν ἐφθέγγετο [Prin ē to deuteron alektryōn ephthengeto], "Before the cock crows a second time," that is, very early in the morning. Synesius, Epist. 4: Ἧς (νυκτὸς) ἤδη περὶ δευτέραν οὔσης ὀρνίθων ᾠδήν [Hēs (nyktos) ēdē peri deuteran ousēs ornithōn ōdēn]; "When the night was already about the second crowing of the cocks." Juvenal, Satire 9, line 106:
"Yet what he does at the crowing of the second cock, the nearest innkeeper will know before daybreak." — —
